Temperature structure of the open ocean: warm surface mixed layer, thermocline, cold deep water
Tides: caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun; most coastal locations get two high and two low tides a day
Waves: wind-driven surface waves; basic anatomy (crest, trough, wavelength); waves transmit energy, not water
Ocean layering by light and the life zones: sunlit (photic), twilight, and midnight zones; the deep sea

Ocean acidification: carbon dioxide dissolving in seawater lowers pH

claims.claim: The average salinity of ocean water is about 35 parts per thousand, which means about 3.5 percent of the weight of seawater comes from dissolved salts.
Chloride and sodium are the two most prevalent ions in seawater, together making up around 85 percent of all dissolved ions; magnesium and sulfate make up another 10 percent.
Salt enters the ocean from two sources: runoff from the land (rocks weathered by rainwater) and openings in the seafloor; salinity varies with temperature, evaporation, and precipitation.
Seawater holds dissolved gases: oxygen is produced in the surface layer by photosynthetic plankton, and carbon dioxide dissolves into the ocean from the atmosphere.
The open ocean has a temperature structure: a warmer, wind-mixed surface layer; a thermocline where temperature decreases rapidly with depth; and cold deep water below.
Cold, salty water is denser than warm water and sinks, which is why the deep ocean stays cold; heat leaking from Earth's interior is negligible at the seafloor.

Tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun; they behave as very long-period waves, and most coastal locations experience two high tides and two low tides each day, usually unequal.
In a tidal wave, the crest brings high tide and the trough brings low tide; the difference in height between high tide and low tide is the tidal range.
Most ocean surface waves are wind-driven, created by friction between wind and surface water; waves transmit energy, not water, and the water moves in a circular motion as the wave passes.

Ocean waves are described by their crests, troughs, and lengths (wavelengths); when swells meet, their crests, troughs, and lengths can line up and reinforce one another to form unusually large waves.

Light divides the ocean into life zones: the sunlit (euphotic) zone is the upper 200 meters and holds the vast majority of commercial fisheries; the twilight (dysphotic) zone spans 200 to 1,000 meters where little light reaches; the aphotic zone below 1,000 meters is dark and includes the midnight zone (1,000-4,000 meters), the abyss (4,000-6,000 meters), and the hadal zone (below 6,000 meters); photosynthesis is not possible below about 200 meters.
About half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, with the majority produced by oceanic plankton — drifting plants, algae, and some bacteria that photosynthesize.
Plankton are marine drifters carried by tides and currents; microscopic phytoplankton perform photosynthesis and play a huge role in the marine food web.
The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface and holds about 97 percent of Earth's water (roughly 1,335,000,000 cubic kilometers of a total of about 1,386,000,000).

Ocean acidification is a reduction in the pH of the ocean over an extended period of time, caused primarily by uptake of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere; the ocean absorbs about 30 percent of the CO2 released into the atmosphere.
When CO2 is absorbed by seawater, chemical reactions increase the concentration of hydrogen ions, making the seawater more acidic and making carbonate ions relatively less abundant.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Ocean coverage of Earth's surface is stated differently across NOAA pages: 'more than 70 percent' (How much water is in the ocean?) versus '71 percent' (Why do scientists measure sea surface temperature?).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are consistent; the lesson uses 'about 71 percent,' citing both pages. Arithmetic noted: 71% is the commonly cited value.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Number of daily tides: an idealized model gives two equal high and low tides everywhere, but real coastlines vary — some places see one high and one low tide a day, and most see two unequal highs.
positions: Two equal high and low tides every day everywhere
Most coastal locations have two high and two low tides a day, usually unequal; some places have one
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the NOAA statement: most coastal locations have two high tides and two low tides a day, and the highs and lows typically are not equal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Share of Earth's oxygen produced by the ocean: estimates vary by source and method.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses NOAA's stated figure: about half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from plankton.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Magnitude of ocean pH change: some summaries cite a drop of about 0.1 pH units since the industrial revolution; the NOAA fact page read for this lesson does not state any drop amount.
positions: No drop amount on the NOAA fact page read
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states only the verified qualitative chemistry (CO2 uptake lowers pH over time, increases hydrogen ions, reduces carbonate ions) and the verified 30 percent CO2 absorption figure. No unverified pH magnitude is taught.

unsupportedExistingClaims: Draft boilerplate 'Ocean Systems is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science' — generic filler with no scientific content or source support.
Draft boilerplate 'College courses use ocean systems as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' — unsupported generic claim.
Draft boilerplate 'A college-level explanation names the concept, describes its parts, and shows how those parts work together' — meta-commentary, not lesson content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate (in30Seconds, whyItMatters, collegeVersion, objectives) with source-verified ocean science.

Added verified quantitative values: average salinity ~35 parts per thousand (3.5%), ocean covers about 71% of Earth's surface, ocean holds about 97% of Earth's water, chloride+sodium ~85% of dissolved ions, light-zone depth boundaries (200 m, 1,000 m, 4,000 m), ocean absorbs about 30% of CO2 released into the atmosphere.

Taught wave anatomy (crest, trough, wavelength) with crest and trough defined from NOAA's tidal-wave text and wavelength as the crest-to-crest length, consistent with NOAA's description of waves by their crests, troughs, and lengths.
Cut pH magnitude claims (e.g., any specific drop in pH units) because the read NOAA source does not state them.
Scoped out ocean circulation, atmosphere-ocean coupling, and climate change, explicitly naming them as sibling topics.

sourceRecords.title: Why is the ocean salty?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: average salinity about 35 parts per thousand, about 3.5 percent of seawater weight from dissolved salts; chloride and sodium as the two most prevalent ions (~85% of dissolved ions) with magnesium and sulfate another ~10%; salt sources of land runoff and seafloor openings; salinity varying with temperature, evaporation, and precipitation. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is a thermocline?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: the thermocline as the transition layer between warmer mixed water at the ocean's surface and cooler deep water, where temperature decreases rapidly from the mixed upper layer (epipelagic) to colder deep water. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Why does the ocean get colder at depth?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: cold water has higher density than warm water; cold, salty water sinks below less dense warm surface water, so the deep ocean is cold; geothermal heat from Earth's interior is negligible for warming the deep ocean. Ocean-circulation mechanics on this page (global conveyor belt) are out of scope and referenced only. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What are tides?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: tides caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun; tides as very long-period waves moving through the ocean in response to forces exerted by the Moon and Sun; crest of the tidal wave bringing high tide and trough bringing low tide; tidal range as the difference in height between high and low tide. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How many high tides are there per day?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: while some places have one high and one low tide per day, most coastal locations have two high tides and two low tides a day, and these highs and lows typically are not equal; the idealized two-equal-tides model applies only to a perfect sphere without continents. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Why does the ocean have waves?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent (the older /facts/waves.html URL redirects to this current URL). Supports: waves created by energy passing through water, causing circular motion; waves transmit energy, not water, and can travel across an entire ocean basin; waves most commonly caused by wind, with wind-driven surface waves created by friction between wind and surface water, forming a wave crest. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is a rogue wave?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports only the general wave-characteristics statement: ocean waves are described by their crests, troughs, and lengths, and when swells pass through one another their crests, troughs, and lengths can coincide and reinforce to form unusually large waves. Rogue-wave lore and hazard content not used. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How far does light travel in the ocean?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports the light-based life zones: euphotic (sunlight) zone in the upper 200 meters, home to the vast majority of commercial fisheries; twilight (dysphotic) zone between 200 and 1,000 meters where photosynthesis is no longer possible; aphotic zone below 1,000 meters, subdivided into the midnight (bathypelagic) zone 1,000-4,000 meters, the abyss 4,000-6,000 meters, and the hadal zone below 6,000 meters. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How much oxygen comes from the ocean?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: about half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, the majority from oceanic plankton (drifting plants, algae, and some bacteria that photosynthesize), with the tiny photosynthesizer Prochlorococcus contributing up to 20% of biosphere oxygen. Used for the oxygen claim only; the specific Prochlorococcus figure is not taught. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What are plankton?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: plankton as marine drifters carried along by tides and currents; microscopic phytoplankton that perform photosynthesis and play a huge role in the marine food web. Used for the food-web claim only. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is Ocean Acidification?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: ocean acidification as a reduction in the pH of the ocean over an extended period, caused primarily by uptake of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere; the ocean absorbs about 30 percent of the CO2 released into the atmosphere; absorbed CO2 triggers chemical reactions that increase hydrogen-ion concentration, making seawater more acidic and carbonate ions relatively less abundant. The page links the atmospheric CO2 rise to fossil-fuel burning and land-use change over more than 200 years, mentioned only as context; climate change is a sibling topic. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Why do scientists measure sea surface temperature?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (NOAA). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21 with a browser user agent. Supports: the ocean covers 71 percent of Earth's surface; sea surface temperature provides fundamental information on the global climate system and how the ocean communicates with the atmosphere. Used for the climate-regulation claim (general, no weather/climate mechanism detail). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How much water is in the ocean?
sourceRecords.notes: Existing source-registry record reused exactly (same id, same URL). Supports: the ocean covers more than 70 percent of Earth's surface; about 97 percent of Earth's water is in the ocean; total Earth water about 1,386,000,000 cubic kilometers and ocean water about 1,335,000,000 cubic kilometers (arithmetic cross-checked: 1,335/1,386 = about 96.3 percent, consistent with the rounded 97 percent). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
